extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and formal-methods researchers (Isabelle/HOL users) working on formal verification and exhaustive computational enumeration (Kepler-conjecture style proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal, machine-checked reworking of the Kepler conjecture proof: executable enumeration of plane/tame graphs, representation of graph systems, and formally verified refutation of potential counterexamples via linear programming certificates inside Isabelle/HOL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding polynomials via Bernstein representation
rubrics_metrics.description: If p(x) = sum_{i=0}^k b_i · B^k_i(x) (Bernstein basis of order k) then ∀x ∈ [0,1]. p(x) ≤ max_i b_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert a polynomial to its Bernstein representation to obtain an upper bound from the largest Bernstein coefficient; reduce any interval to [0,1] by change of variable; multivariate generalization is straightforward. For practical purposes use an efficient algorithm (cf. [6,48]) rather than naive matrix multiplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling transcendental/irrational coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: g contains irrational coefficients (consequence of requirement (5.1)); approximation polynomials were chosen so the transcendental parts factor out (e.g. occurrence of π−4 arctan in definition of sqrt), and p(y) := 2(g(y) − pt) has rational coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When p has rational coefficients it can be converted to a Bernstein representation without rounding using the algorithm in [48]; only divisions by powers of 2 occur and dyadic numbers can represent these exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent plane graphs as lists of faces (faces as oriented vertex lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite, undirected, plane graphs are represented as lists (= finite sets) of faces, and faces are lists of vertices (hence oriented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because faces are lists they carry an orientation. Enumeration requires distinguishing final and non-final faces, so a face is a pair (list_of_vertices, Boolean). A plane graph is final iff each of its faces is final; in final graphs the Boolean component can be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define planarity by executable enumeration (next-planep / Seedp)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original proof's executable enumeration is taken as the definition of planarity: start from a seed graph (Seedp) and apply next-planep inductively to subdivide non-final faces until final graphs (leaves) are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seedp contains two (p+3)-gons; a plane graph of n faces can be generated in n−1 steps by adding one final face at a time. The Bernstein of order p parameterizes maximal size of final faces; different p produce disjoint graph sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration parameter p (face-size control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The enumeration is parameterized by natural number p which controls the maximal size of final faces in the generated graphs (final faces are at most (p+3)-gons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tame graphs may contain only triangles up to octagons, corresponding to parameters p = 0,...,5; enumeration is run for these p values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executable successor function next-tamep for tame enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The HOL formalization defines next-tamep which maps a graph to a list of successors by computing next-planep and post-processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: next-tamep post-processes next-planep results by: (1) removing graphs that cannot lead to tame graphs due to lower bound admissible weight estimates; (2) finalizing all triangles (every 3-cycle in a tame graph must be a face); (3) removing final graphs that are not tame (a necessary but possibly not sufficient check). The enumeration may produce non-tame graphs (acceptable: may yield fake counterexamples but won't miss real ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pruning effectiveness with formal simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pruning criteria must be chosen to balance execution efficiency and ease of formal completeness proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak pruning criteria are easy to justify formally but slow; sophisticated pruning is faster but harder to justify. Prefer simplifications that make formal proofs manageable even if they forego complex optimizations (e.g., removed special treatment of Seed0 and Seed1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive construction and isomorphism elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of running tameEnump for p=0..5 are collected into an Archive and isomorphic graphs are eliminated, producing a reduced Archive (2771 graphs versus 5128 in original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced Archive differences are due to isomorphic copies and non-tame graphs that the original program did not enforce; to build on enumeration results without rerunning, store and deduplicate outputs and verify modulo graph isomorphism (verified executable test for graph isomorphism is available in HOL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic must contain an executable programming language (HOL)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic must contain a programming language; we used Church’s higher-order logic (HOL) based on λ-calculus, where programs are sets of recursion equations (pure logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets programs be written as logical definitions (recursion equations) and reasoned about inside the logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executions must be efficient and count as proofs (Isabelle/HOL evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The programming language contained in the logic must be efficiently executable and such executions must count as proofs: Isabelle/HOL can evaluate a term t to a value v and yield the theorem t = v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all functions in a term are data or defined by recursion equations, Isabelle/HOL can 'evaluate' the term in one efficient step producing a machine-checked equality theorem; this makes large computations part of the formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent tame graphs as hypermaps (darts + permutations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tame graphs are represented as hypermaps: a finite set D of darts with three permutations (edge, face, node) composing to identity e ◦ n ◦ f = I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representation simplifies the axiomatization of a graph system and the formal development; see [38, §4] for full axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph system axioms → large conjunction of linear (in)equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the axioms of a graph system to each tame graph to obtain a large Isabelle theorem: a conjunction of linear equalities and inequalities which is normalized into a matrix inequality Ax ≤ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries of A and b are symbolic expressions that may contain real constants (e.g., π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal interval arithmetic to bound symbolic matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace A and b with numerical approximations A', A'' and b' with formally proven bounds: A' ≤ A ≤ A'' and b ≤ b'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal interval-arithmetic development in Isabelle is used to obtain these numerical matrices with machine-checked inequalities (Equation (5) style bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute formal a-priori bounds for variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply preprocessing to obtain formally proven a-priori bounds x' ≤ x ≤ x'' for x such that x' ≤ x ≤ x''.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bounds are used to confine variable ranges before applying linear programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external LP solver certificates verifiably
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a certificate from an external LP solver (e.g., GLPK) that can be checked inside Isabelle to derive a contradiction from Ax ≤ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certificates allow use of heavily optimized, untrusted solvers while retaining a trusted, mechanically verifiable final check in Isabelle; this yields soundness even with untrusted external code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current formalization limited to constraints avoiding branch-and-bound
rubrics_metrics.description: The present formalization does not use all constraints of the original proof but only those that do not require branch-and-bound strategies; this notion corresponds to 'basic linear programs' in [22, §23.3].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because not all constraints are captured, not all potential counterexamples can be refuted yet; nevertheless most are refuted (2565 out of 2771, ≈92.5%). Future work will extend the notion of graph system to include remaining constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of edges E (construction rules and special edges S)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edges E' between vertices in U are formed from: (i) all standard edges {v,w} with 0 < ||v−w|| ≤ 2.51; (ii) edges {v,w} of an anchored simplex when the upright diagonal is an unerased loop; (iii) edges with 0 < ||v−w|| ≤ √8 provided they do not cross any edge in previous two items (if crossing choose one). Special simplices have a special edge of length at most √8 and at least 3.2; S is the set of special edges and E = E' \ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By construction these edges do not cross; projecting E to the unit sphere yields a planar graph whose complementary components' closures are subregions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loop subregion characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A loop subregion contains an unerased loop {0,v}; it has no enclosed vertices of height ≤ 2.51 over the subregion; its corners are anchors of the upright diagonal together with special corners; the subregion is star-convex with center at the projection of v and has a simple polygonal boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures loop subregions' boundaries are simple polygons and remain rigid under admissible deformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible deformation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformation of U is admissible if: (i) if Γ is not connected, the deformation is a rotation about the origin acting on vertices of a single connected component (others fixed) (preserves ||v||); (ii) if Γ is connected but not biconnected with articulation vertex a, deform by rotation about axis {0,a} acting on a single component of Γ\{a} (others fixed); (iii) distances between any v,w ∈ U remain at least 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deformations are constructed to preserve values of vor0,R and τ0,R for standard regions while changing combinatorial structure to reach biconnectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible deformation halting conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The deformation stops when either: (1) ||v−w|| ≤ √8 where edge {v,w} ∉ E' and {v,w} ⊆ U does not cross any edge in E'; or (2) ||v−w|| decreases to 2 for some v,w ∈ U and {v,w} crosses an edge in E'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deformation is allowed to assume configurations where distances between some u ∈ U and the upper endpoint of an unerased upright diagonal dip below 2, provided u is not a corner of that loop subregion; the first halting condition prevents adding new special vertices to a loop subregion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: produce biconnected graph to ensure polygonal faces
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof strategy is to produce a biconnected graph; in a biconnected planar graph with at least three vertices each face is a simple polygon, thereby justifying reduction to polygonal standard regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with erasure simplification, then admissible deformations preserving vor0,R and τ0,R while altering combinatorial structure to eliminate articulation vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of necessary-but-not-sufficient tameness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: In the last step of next-tamep, a necessary but possibly not sufficient check for tameness is used, so enumeration may produce non-tame graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is unproblematic: in worst case one gets a fake counterexample, but one does not miss any real counterexamples. The completeness theorem (Theorem 2) guarantees that any tame final graph reachable by next-planep is also reachable by next-tamep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metric lemmas/explicit metric thresholds to exclude pathological configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of geometric lemmas with explicit numerical thresholds (e.g., distances ≥2, ≤2.51, ≤3.2, ≤2.91, diameter bounds like 1.044, dihedral/distance interval calculations) is used to rule out configurations that would obstruct admissible deformations or biconnectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metric constraints are explicit parts of the formal proof (Lemmas 1–12) and must be checked by geometric calculation/interval arithmetic or coordinate computations inside the formal system; they underpin elimination of hypothetical problematic cases (Figs. 2–4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness theorem for tame enumeration (Theorem 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tame and final graph g is reachable from Seedp via next-planep then g is also reachable from Seedp via next-tamep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because next-tamep is executable and exhaustive (modulo its pruning), tameEnump can be used to enumerate tame graphs for p=0..5 and the resulting set checked modulo isomorphism against the Archive.
